question_en: Do I need an FSSAI licence to serve breakfast and meals to my homestay guests?
answer: The Food Safety Act treats any undertaking that handles food as a food business, whether or not it earns a profit. The FSSAI papers I read do not have a special rule for homestays. So the safe step is to ask your food safety office which registration or licence fits your set-up. From 1 April 2026, small businesses with yearly turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore fall in the basic registration band.
actions: Write down how many guests you feed per day, which meals you serve, and your yearly food income.
Call the FSSAI helpline 1800112100 or your District Food Safety Officer and describe your set-up.
Apply on the FoSCoS portal (foscos.fssai.gov.in) for the category they confirm.
caution: Do not assume that serving only a few guests means no rule applies. Also do not guess the category yourself; caterers are treated differently from petty operators in the regulations.
context_needed: whether guests pay separately for food
evidence: FSS Act 2006 s.3(1)(n) definition (for profit or not), s.31; 2026 band from FSSAI FAQ dated 27 Mar 2026; no homestay-specific FSSAI text found
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I heard FSSAI changed the limits in 2026. What are the new registration and licence limits?
answer: From 1 April 2026: basic registration is for yearly turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore. A State licence is for turnover above Rs 1.5 crore and up to Rs 50 crore. A Central licence is for turnover above Rs 50 crore. The old registration limit was Rs 12 lakh.
actions: Add up your yearly food sales to see which band you fall in.
Check on FoSCoS or with your Food Safety Officer if any other condition applies to your kind of business.
caution: Some businesses (for example dairy, meat, packaged drinking water, infant food, fish) still have to meet full hygiene and testing rules whatever their band. Ask your Food Safety Officer about your product.
evidence: FSSAI press release 13 Mar 2026 and FSSAI FAQs 27 Mar 2026: registration up to Rs 1.5 crore; State above Rs 1.5 crore to Rs 50 crore; Central above Rs 50 crore; effective 1 Apr 2026
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Do I still have to renew my FSSAI registration or licence every year?
answer: From 1 April 2026, FSSAI registrations and licences stay valid until they are suspended, cancelled or surrendered. You no longer need to renew them. Your hygiene and safety duties continue. You can pay fees for any number of years at once.
actions: Keep your registration or licence number safe and displayed.
Pay the fee on FoSCoS when it is due and keep the receipt.
Keep following the hygiene rules and be ready for inspection.
caution: Perpetual validity does not cancel duties such as fees, returns for licensed manufacturers, or hygiene rules. Non-compliance can still lead to suspension.
context_needed: whether you hold registration or licence
evidence: FSSAI FAQs 27 Mar 2026 Q4, Q5: perpetual validity unless suspended, cancelled or surrendered; fee for any number of years
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What does 'petty food business operator' mean? Am I one?
answer: The regulations name small operators as petty: for example a petty retailer, hawker, itinerant (moving) vendor, temporary stall holder, or a small manufacturer. Petty operators get registration and follow the lighter Part I hygiene rules. The older text lists caterers as not petty. The money limit for the basic registration band is now Rs 1.5 crore a year.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer whether your activity counts as petty or as catering.
Read the Part I hygiene checklist and follow it in your kitchen.
caution: The older regulation text also had daily capacity limits (such as 100 kg or litres a day). I could not confirm in 2026 papers whether those limits still apply. Ask the office.
evidence: FSSAI Licensing Regulations compendium (2017) petty food manufacturer definition (excludes caterer); FSS Act s.31(2) petty operators register; 2026 band from FAQ 27 Mar 2026
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Is there still a limit on how much food I can make per day to stay in registration?
answer: The 2022 FSSAI FAQ says registration was for turnover up to Rs 12 lakh AND production up to 100 kg or litres a day, milk handling up to 500 litres a day, or slaughter up to 2 large animals, 10 small animals or 50 poultry birds a day. The 2026 papers I read only talk about turnover bands. I could not confirm whether the daily limits still apply.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer if daily quantity limits apply to your product.
Note how much you make per day at peak season before you call.
caution: Do not rely on the old Rs 12 lakh figure; it was replaced from 1 April 2026.
evidence: FSSAI FAQs 26 Jul 2022 (old criteria) versus FAQs 27 Mar 2026 (turnover bands only); conflict not resolved
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I cook meals for tourist groups and village events. Am I a caterer and what licence do I need?
answer: FSSAI says caterers for marriages and parties must obtain a licence or registration as per the eligibility criteria. The older regulation text treats a caterer as outside the petty category. A secondary source says caterers need at least a State licence, but I could not confirm that on an FSSAI page. So ask your food safety office before you start.
actions: Tell your Food Safety Officer how many people you cook for, how often, and whether you cook at your place or at the guests' place.
Apply on FoSCoS for the category they advise.
caution: Licensed caterers are expected to follow Schedule 4 Part V (catering) hygiene rules, which are stricter than Part I.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 2022 Q74 (caterers shall obtain licence or registration as per eligibility); Licensing Regulations compendium 2017 (petty definition excludes caterer); State-licence minimum for caterers only from a secondary source (unconfirmed)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I run a village cooking class where guests cook and eat with me. Do I need FSSAI registration?
answer: The papers I read do not give a special rule for cooking classes. If guests eat the food you prepare, it is likely to be treated as a food business, because the Act covers businesses 'whether for profit or not'. The right category depends on your turnover and set-up. Ask your food safety office, and describe the class exactly.
actions: Describe your class (number of guests, price, who cooks, who eats) to your District Food Safety Officer.
Follow the kitchen hygiene steps in this bank even before the licence decision.
caution: Do not wait for an inspection to start good hygiene. Guests may be sick if food is mishandled.
evidence: FSS Act 2006 s.3(1)(n) 'whether for profit or not'; no cooking-class-specific FSSAI text found
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: My farm serves lunch to visitors with vegetables from our field. Is that covered by FSSAI?
answer: Selling your own crop is one thing, but cooking and serving a meal is food service. The FSSAI FAQ I read does not address farmers' primary produce or farm meals directly. Treat the meal as a food business and ask your food safety office for the right category.
actions: Ask your District Food Safety Officer if serving cooked meals on your farm needs registration or licence.
Keep a simple record of where your vegetables and other ingredients come from.
caution: Rules for selling raw farm produce may differ from rules for cooked meals. Do not assume an exemption.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 2022: no Q&A on primary producers or farm meals found; FSS Act s.3(1)(n)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Our women's self-help group makes pickle, jam and masala. Who needs registration, the group or each woman?
answer: The FSSAI FAQ says individual members who work from their homes for a registered cooperative society, Gruh Udyog, Mahila Udyog, SHG or similar government-registered society do not need separate FSSAI registration. This follows an FSSAI order dated 21 January 2015. The society or group itself still has to meet the rules for its products.
actions: Check that your group is registered under a government scheme or society law and keep the proof.
Ask your Food Safety Officer to confirm the group's own registration or licence category.
Put the group's FSSAI number on each product label.
caution: The exemption is for members working from home for the group. It does not remove hygiene or labelling duties.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 26 Jul 2022 Q12 (order 03-01/2012/Enf-I/FSSAI dated 21 Jan 2015)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I want to run a small dhaba or tiffin service in the village. Which FSSAI category do I need?
answer: A dhaba, tea stall or tiffin service is a food business. Under the 2026 bands, small businesses up to Rs 1.5 crore a year fall under basic registration, subject to your food type and the rules for your kind of business. FSSAI also says cloud kitchens (no seating) need a licence or registration as per eligibility. On FoSCoS you choose the Kind of Business and then the food product category.
actions: Decide your Kind of Business on FoSCoS (for example food service or food vending).
Ask your Food Safety Officer to confirm the category and what hygiene part applies.
Keep your turnover records.
caution: Licensed food service outlets follow Schedule 4 Part V. Registered petty operators follow Part I.
evidence: FSSAI FAQs 27 Mar 2026 (bands); FAQ 2022 Q77 (cloud kitchens) and Q97 (Kind of Business choice)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: We want to set up a food stall for three days at the village mela. Do we need a licence?
answer: Yes, some approval is needed even for a temporary stall. Since 1 August 2025, FoSCoS can give a seasonal registration for short events such as religious fairs and food festivals. It is valid for up to 3 months and cannot be renewed. The fee is Rs 100, and hawkers are exempt from the fee. It is meant for retailers, petty snack and tea shops, hawkers and food vending establishments.
actions: Apply for seasonal registration through your food safety office or FoSCoS before the fair.
Carry a copy of the registration to the stall.
Follow the hygiene steps for stalls (clean water, covered food, handwashing).
caution: The order says it applies to short events and is not renewable. Do not run a year-round stall on it.
evidence: FSSAI Order 15 Oct 2025 (F. No. 15(31)2020/FoSCoS/RCD/FSSAIpt1): seasonal registration up to 3 months, non-renewable, Rs 100, effective 1 Aug 2025
verify_with: Your District Food Safety Officer or Designated Officer

question_en: Our village temple gives prasad and runs a bhandara. Does it need FSSAI registration?
answer: Yes. The FSSAI FAQ says temples offering prasad, or organising langar or bhandara, shall obtain an FSSAI licence or registration as per the eligibility criteria.
actions: Ask the temple committee to apply on FoSCoS for the right category.
Follow the same hygiene steps (clean water, covered food, clean cooks) for the bhandara.
caution: Category depends on turnover and scale. Ask your Food Safety Officer.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 26 Jul 2022 Q75
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: We sell our pickles and snacks through WhatsApp and Instagram. Do we still need FSSAI?
answer: FSSAI says food businesses that sell through their own e-commerce platform must obtain the licence under the e-Commerce category too. Sellers on e-commerce platforms must display their licence or registration number. The FAQs I read do not mention WhatsApp or Instagram sales. Treat them as food sales and ask your food safety office.
actions: Get your registration or licence first, then show the number on every pack and online listing.
Ask your Food Safety Officer if your online selling needs an extra category.
caution: Packed food also needs a proper label, even if it is sold only through social media.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 2022 Q80 (own e-commerce platform needs e-Commerce licence); 2018 notice: sellers on platforms must display licence/registration; social media not addressed
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How do I apply for FSSAI registration? Which portal and which documents?
answer: Applications are made on the FoSCoS portal (Food Safety Compliance System) at foscos.fssai.gov.in. Registration uses Form A. The list of documents depends on your Kind of Business and is shown on the FoSCoS home page under 'Documents Required'. After you apply, you log in with your registration or licence number or application reference number.
actions: Open the 'Documents Required' list on FoSCoS for your Kind of Business and collect those papers.
Choose the correct Kind of Business and food product category.
Ask your local food safety office or the helpline 1800112100 if you get stuck.
caution: Beware of agents who charge large fees. The government fee for registration is small (see the fee row).
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 2022 Q41 (documents list on FoSCoS) and Q127 (login); Form A via FoSCoS in Oct 2025 order; helpline 1800112100
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How much does FSSAI registration cost?
answer: The regulation text I read sets the registration fee at Rs 100, and the 2025 seasonal registration order also says Rs 100 (hawkers exempt). Fees for State and Central licences depend on the business and are shown on FoSCoS before you pay. Since 2026 you can pay for any number of years at once.
actions: Check the exact fee on FoSCoS before paying.
Pay only through the official portal and keep the receipt.
caution: The Rs 100 in the regulation compendium is from the 2017 version. Confirm the current amount on FoSCoS.
evidence: Licensing Regulations compendium 2017 (registration Rs 100); FSSAI Order 15 Oct 2025 (Rs 100 for seasonal); FSSAI FAQ 27 Mar 2026 Q5 (pay for any number of years)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I want to start serving food to guests. What should I do first?
answer: Start with three things in this order: (1) find out your FSSAI category with your food safety office, (2) fix the basics in your kitchen (clean water, handwashing, covered storage, pest control), (3) apply on FoSCoS. Do the kitchen basics now; they do not depend on the licence.
actions: Call the FSSAI helpline 1800112100 or your District Food Safety Officer and ask which category fits you.
Check your kitchen against the hygiene steps in this bank.
Apply on FoSCoS and keep the certificate where guests can see it.
caution: Do not serve paying guests until you know what approval you need.
evidence: General sequence built from FSS Act s.31 and Schedule 4 Part I; helpline from FSSAI helpdesk page
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Which government office do I go to for FSSAI registration or a food question?
answer: Licences are given by Designated Officers under the Food Safety Act, and inspections are done by Food Safety Officers. Both sit in your district food safety office under your state Food Safety Commissioner. You can also call FSSAI's toll-free helpline 1800112100 (24x7).
actions: Ask your Gram Panchayat or block office where the District Food Safety Officer sits.
Call 1800112100 if you cannot find the office.
Do the application online on FoSCoS and visit the office only if they ask.
caution: Office names and locations differ by state. Check with your district.
evidence: FSS Act s.31 (licence issued by Designated Officer), s.38 (Food Safety Officer); helpline 1800112100 on FSSAI helpdesk page
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What happens if I serve or sell food without FSSAI registration? Will the police come?
answer: Running a food business without the registration or licence you need is an offence under the Food Safety Act (section 63). FSSAI also says working on a suspended or cancelled licence is unlawful and leads to penal action. The exact penalty amounts have been changed in recent years and I could not confirm the current figures, so ask the food safety office.
actions: Apply for the right registration or licence as soon as you can.
If you have already started, speak to the Food Safety Officer yourself and ask how to regularise.
caution: Do not rely on rumours about fine amounts. Ask the office or a local lawyer.
evidence: FSS Act s.63 exists; FSSAI FAQ 2022 Q5 on unlawful activity; amounts not stated because sources conflict
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer; a local lawyer for legal advice

question_en: Do I need to display my FSSAI certificate? Where?
answer: Yes. A licence holder must display a true copy of the licence at a prominent place in the premises at all times. Keep your registration certificate ready too, and show your FSSAI number on packs and online listings if you sell them.
actions: Frame your certificate and fix it near the entrance or the dining area.
Keep a photo copy and a digital copy in case it is damaged.
caution: Rules for displaying registration (not licence) were not stated in the pages I read. Ask your Food Safety Officer.
evidence: Licensing Regulations compendium 2017, conditions of licence: display a true copy of the licence at a prominent place
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What is the FSSAI Food Safety Display Board and do I need one?
answer: The 2018 restaurant licence conditions say licensed restaurants must display a Food Safety Display Board at a prominent place. I did not find an FSSAI page saying small registered homestays or stalls must have it. Ask your Food Safety Officer.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer whether your category needs the board.
Download the format from FoSCoS or FSSAI if you are told to use it.
caution: Do not buy a board from a private seller before the office confirms you need it.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice, Section III (conditions of licence for restaurants): Food Safety Display Board
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What records should I keep in my kitchen for FSSAI?
answer: Schedule 4 Part V asks you to keep records of raw materials and where you got them, and to label stored prepared food with date and time. Production and distribution records should be legible and kept for one year or the shelf life of the product, whichever is longer. Keep water test and food test reports too.
actions: Keep a notebook of purchases with the shop name and date.
Write date and time on every container of prepared food you store.
File your water test and medical fitness papers in one folder.
caution: Licensed manufacturers also have returns to file. Ask the office what applies to you.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice: Part V 2.1.6 (raw material records), 2.3.5 (date and time tag), 2.10.3 (test records); Part II records for one year or shelf life
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Our group has an FSSAI licence for making pickles. Do we have to file any yearly return?
answer: FSSAI says licensed manufacturers (including repackers and relabellers) must submit an annual return in Form D1 by 31 May. Late filing attracts a late fee of Rs 100 a day. The 2026 reform notes say fees and mandatory returns still need to be kept up.
actions: Mark 31 May in your calendar and file the return on FoSCoS.
Ask your Food Safety Officer whether the return rule changed for your category in 2026.
caution: This answer is from the 2022 FAQ. Check the latest rule on FoSCoS.
evidence: FSSAI FAQ 2022 Q47, Q48 (Form D1 by 31 May, Rs 100 per day late fee); 2026 FAQ says obligations continue
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: A Food Safety Officer is coming to inspect my kitchen. What should I expect and how should I behave?
answer: Under the Food Safety Act, a Food Safety Officer can enter and inspect any place where food is made or stored for sale, take samples, and seize food that looks unsafe. Since 2026 FSSAI plans risk-based inspections, so places with a good record are visited less. Be calm, help them, and show your papers.
actions: Keep your certificate, purchase records and water test report ready.
Walk with the officer, answer honestly, and write down what they ask for.
Ask for a written copy of anything they take or any notice they issue.
caution: Do not hide food or refuse entry. If you are unsure of your rights, ask a local lawyer or the helpline.
evidence: FSS Act s.38 (enter, inspect, sample, seize); FSSAI press release 13 Mar 2026 (risk-based inspections)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: The officer gave me an improvement notice. What does it mean?
answer: The Act lets an officer serve an improvement notice if the rules are not followed. The notice says what you must fix and gives at least fourteen days. If you do not fix it, your licence can be suspended or cancelled.
actions: Read the notice and list each thing to fix.
Fix them within the time and keep photos and bills as proof.
Reply in writing and ask the office to confirm when you have fixed everything.
caution: If you disagree, get advice from a local lawyer. This is general information and not legal advice.
evidence: FSS Act s.32 (improvement notice, not less than fourteen days)
verify_with: Designated Officer who issued the notice

question_en: The officer took a sample of my food. What happens next?
answer: A Food Safety Officer can take samples of food meant for sale and send them for lab testing. The result decides if the food meets the rules. If the food fails, there can be a penalty or a case.
actions: Ask for the sample receipt and keep it.
Note the product, batch and date of the sample.
Ask the office how you will be told the result.
caution: I could not confirm the exact steps and timelines on an official page. Take local legal advice if a notice arrives.
evidence: FSS Act s.38 (FSO may take a sample); detailed procedure not verified
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer; a local lawyer

question_en: A guest says my food made them ill and wants it tested. Can they do that?
answer: Yes, in some cases. The Act lets a purchaser get food analysed by a Food Analyst by paying the fee, if they tell the seller at the time of purchase. The fee is refunded if the food is found not to meet the rules. A guest can also complain to FSSAI on 1800112100.
actions: Listen to the guest calmly and note down what they ate and when.
Keep a sample of the suspect food if you still have it (see the food poisoning row).
Cooperate with the Food Safety Officer if they contact you.
caution: Do not argue or hide the food. Take any illness seriously and help the guest get medical care.
evidence: FSS Act s.40 (purchaser may have food analysed); FSSAI helpline 1800112100
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What is the FSSAI helpline number? Where can I complain or ask a licence question?
answer: FSSAI's toll-free helpline is 1800112100. It works 24x7 for food complaints and licensing or registration problems. FSSAI also takes complaints through its app, website, WhatsApp and social media channels; check fssai.gov.in for the current links.
actions: Save 1800112100 in your phone.
Use the number to ask about licence status or to report unsafe food.
caution: I did not verify any other phone number or WhatsApp number, so none is given here.
evidence: FSSAI helpdesk page: 1800112100, 24x7
verify_with: FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: If my sales grow beyond the limit, do I have to apply again and pay more?
answer: FSSAI says businesses are moved to the right band automatically on FoSCoS using your own self-declaration, with no approval needed. No fee is charged for moves caused by the 2026 limit changes, and your licence number stays the same. If your category changes later, fees you already paid are adjusted.
actions: Update your turnover details honestly on FoSCoS.
Keep your sales records so you can show your turnover.
caution: This is from the 2026 FAQ. Ask the office if you add new products such as dairy or meat.
evidence: FSSAI FAQs 27 Mar 2026 Q6, Q7, Q10, Q11
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Our village haat vendors are registered with the panchayat or town vending committee. Do they also need FSSAI registration?
answer: Since the 2026 reform, street food vendors, hawkers, food carts and food trucks registered under the Street Vendors Act, 2014 are treated as deemed registered under food safety law. This stops double registration. They must still keep food safe and clean.
actions: Ask the vending committee for the vendors' registration papers.
Ask your Food Safety Officer how the vendors should show they are covered.
caution: This applies to vendors registered with a Municipal Corporation or Town Vending Committee. Check how your area handles it.
evidence: FSSAI press release 13 Mar 2026 and FAQs 27 Mar 2026 Q8
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: FSSAI has Schedule 4 hygiene rules. Which part applies to a small village kitchen?
answer: Schedule 4 has parts. Part I is for small (petty) operators who register. Part II is the general hygiene rule for licensed businesses. Part V adds rules for catering and food service on top of Part II. Parts III and IV are for milk and meat. Registered small kitchens follow Part I; licensed food service outlets follow Part II and Part V.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer which part applies to you.
Use the hygiene rows in this bank as a checklist for your kitchen.
caution: Even if only Part I applies, the Part V temperature and handwashing rules are good practice for any kitchen.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice (Part II, IV, V) and Licensing Regulations compendium 2017 (Part I to IV headings); Assam FDA copy of Part I
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What are the basic hygiene rules for a small registered kitchen?
answer: Part I asks for these basics: a clean place free from filth, good light and air, a continuous supply of safe drinking-quality water, and easy-to-clean equipment. Cooks must keep nails trimmed, wear clean aprons and head cover, and wash hands with soap. Sick people must not work, and cuts must be covered. Windows and doors need nets or screens, stored food must be covered, and waste must go out properly.
actions: Check each item above in your kitchen today and fix what is missing.
Fit nets or screens on windows and doors.
Keep a covered bin and empty it every day.
caution: This is the older Part I text hosted by the Assam food safety department. Ask your own state office if it has extra rules.
evidence: Schedule 4 Part I as reproduced by FDA Assam: premises, water, equipment, personnel, medical, pests, storage, waste
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What water can I use for cooking, washing food and making ice?
answer: Part V says to use safe (potable) water for cooking, preparing and steaming food, making ice and drinking. Its quality must meet the BIS standard IS 10500. Water tanks must be food-grade, built to prevent contamination and kept clean. Do not use untested pond, stream or open-well water for guests.
actions: Test your water source (see the water testing row).
Clean the storage tank on a fixed schedule and cover it.
Make ice only from safe water.
caution: If your water is not safe, boil or treat it, and fix the source. Ask your local water authority.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice, Part V 1.4.1: potable water per IS 10500 for cooking, ice and drinking; storage facilities food-grade and maintained
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How often should I test my kitchen water, and where?
answer: The FSSAI text I read gives two different frequencies: Part V says test water samples at least semi-annually in one place and annually in another. Since they differ, test at least twice a year to be safe and ask the food safety office. Village water can be tested through the Jal Jeevan Mission system, which uses Field Test Kits (FTK) with trained village women and laboratories, including NABL-accredited labs.
actions: Ask your Gram Panchayat or the Public Health Engineering / water supply office about FTK testing in your village.
Send a sample to an accredited laboratory once or twice a year and keep the report.
caution: A field kit is a quick check only. Ask the lab which tests (germs and chemicals) you need.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 1.4.1(iii) semi-annually and 2.10.1 annually (conflict); JJM WQMIS page shows FTK and laboratory testing
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What does FSSAI say about toilets and handwashing basins?
answer: Part V says enough toilets of clean design must be available, each with handwashing and drying facilities (and sanitising where needed), and connected to proper drainage. There must also be handwash basins with water for cooks.
actions: Keep a handwash basin with soap and clean water near the kitchen and the toilet.
Clean the toilets every day and record it on a simple chart.
caution: Toilets must not open directly into the food area. Ask the office if your layout is unusual.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V: adequate toilets with hand-washing, drying; 1.4.4 handwash basins
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How do I keep rats, flies and insects out of my kitchen?
answer: Part II/V rules: keep buildings in good repair, seal holes and drains where pests can enter, store food in pest-proof containers, and stack it above the ground and away from walls. Check the premises regularly for signs of pests and set traps or detectors at key places.
actions: Seal holes and fit nets on windows and doors.
Keep food in closed containers and off the floor.
Check corners and stores weekly and note findings.
caution: Use pest chemicals carefully and never near open food. Follow the product label.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part II pest control; Part I (nets and screens)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How should I handle kitchen waste to follow food safety rules?
answer: Part V says food waste and rubbish must not pile up in food areas. Waste bins should be big enough, leak-proof, easy to clean, clearly marked and kept closed (preferably foot-operated). Waste must be disposed of hygienically as per local rules. Drains should not let wastewater back up.
actions: Use a covered bin and empty it daily.
Ask your Gram Panchayat where and how to dispose of food and other waste.
Keep drains clear and clean.
caution: Local disposal rules differ. Ask your Gram Panchayat.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 1.4.2 waste containers and disposal
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: When must cooks and helpers wash hands and what should they not wear?
answer: All people handling food must wash hands with soap and safe water before starting work and after handling chemicals or after touching unsuitable items (such as raw meat). Jewellery, watches and pins should not be worn in food areas if they can harm food safety. Cuts and burns must be covered with waterproof dressings (preferably coloured). Wear clean work clothes, head cover and footwear.
actions: Put soap and a towel (or paper) next to the cooking area.
Ask helpers to remove rings and bangles before cooking.
Keep a first-aid box with coloured waterproof plasters.
caution: Wash hands after using the toilet, handling garbage, and touching your face or phone too.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part II/V personal hygiene: handwashing, jewellery, waterproof dressings, work clothing
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: A family member who cooks has diarrhoea or fever. Can they still cook for guests?
answer: No. FSSAI says employees must report jaundice, diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, sore throat with fever or visibly infected sores to management, so they can be kept out of food areas. The same sense applies to family members who cook for guests.
actions: Keep the sick person away from cooking and serving until a doctor says they are fit.
Let another healthy person cook, or tell guests about a delay.
Wash and clean all surfaces they touched.
caution: If several people in your house are ill, call a doctor and stop serving food until it is clear.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part II/V: illness reporting list for exclusion from food areas
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Do my cooks need a medical certificate?
answer: Part V says food handlers should be examined by a registered medical practitioner every year to ensure they are free from infectious and other communicable diseases. This is written for licensed catering and food service outlets. Ask your office whether it applies to your registration.
actions: Take cooks to a registered doctor once a year and keep the signed report.
Keep the report in your records folder.
caution: Whether the check is required for registered petty operators was not clear in the pages I read.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V: annual medical examination by registered medical practitioner
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How should I clean chopping boards, knives and utensils?
answer: Part V says food-contact surfaces such as chopping boards, knives and peelers must be cleaned thoroughly and disinfected when needed. Method: scrape off food, rinse, wash with warm water and detergent, then rinse with clean water. It names 50 ppm chlorine for vegetarian cutting boards and 100 ppm chlorine for non-vegetarian boards. Keep a cleaning schedule and clean spills after every session.
actions: Use separate boards for vegetarian and non-vegetarian food.
Wash with detergent and rinse, then disinfect boards as shown.
Write a simple cleaning schedule and fix it in the kitchen.
caution: Chlorine must be measured and used as the maker says. If you do not know how to mix ppm, ask a trained supervisor.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.3.4, 3.1.1 to 3.1.5
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How should I store raw ingredients and cooked food?
answer: Part V says store food in dry, well-ventilated areas protected from dust, drips, drains and waste. Keep raw material apart from semi-finished and cooked food, and raw meat, fish and poultry apart from other food. Vegetarian and non-vegetarian food must be kept separate. Use first-in-first-out, and first-expired-first-out. Prepared food kept for later must be labelled with date and time.
actions: Label every container with the date and time.
Keep non-veg items on the lowest shelf, covered and apart from veg and cooked food.
Check dates every week and throw out expired items.
caution: Do not store food on the floor or near chemicals.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.2.1 to 2.2.9, 2.3.5
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What fridge and freezer temperatures does FSSAI give? How do I thaw frozen food?
answer: Part V gives these official figures: refrigerated food of animal origin at 4 deg C or less; foods meant to be eaten cold at 5 deg C or below; frozen items at minus 18 deg C or below. Thaw meat, poultry and fish in a fridge at 5 deg C or in a microwave. Seafood can be thawed in running safe water at 15 deg C or less for no more than 90 minutes. Do not refreeze food after thawing.
actions: Put a thermometer in your fridge and note the reading daily.
Thaw meat in the fridge on a lower shelf.
Do not refreeze thawed food.
caution: If power cuts are common in your village, plan for it. Throw away food if the fridge warmed up for long.
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How do I handle meat, fish and eggs safely for guests?
answer: Part V says to keep raw meat, fish and poultry separate from other food, use separate boards, and keep animal-origin food refrigerated at 4 deg C or less. Cook non-vegetarian food to a core temperature of 75 deg C for 15 seconds (or 65 deg C for 10 minutes). Buy meat and fish from licensed sellers. I did not find FSSAI egg-specific figures, so treat eggs as animal-origin food and keep them cool and well cooked.
actions: Buy from a shop that shows its FSSAI number.
Use a probe thermometer and check that the middle of the food reaches 75 deg C.
Wash hands and boards after touching raw meat, fish or eggs.
caution: Egg storage temperature was not verified on an official page. Ask your Food Safety Officer.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.2.3, 2.2.5, 2.4.2; eggs not specifically covered
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How long can cooked food stay out on the buffet or the table?
answer: Part V says hot food for serving must be kept at 65 deg C or above and cold food at 5 deg C or below. Hot food can be kept below 65 deg C for up to 2 hours, but only once. Cold food can be above 5 deg C but below 10 deg C for up to 2 hours, also only once. After that it must be thrown away.
actions: Keep food hot in covered containers over heat, or serve it fresh from the pot.
Write the time you put food out.
Throw away food that has been out beyond the time limit.
caution: If in doubt, throw it away.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.5.2, 2.5.3, 2.7.4 to 2.7.6
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I reheat leftover food and serve it again to guests?
answer: Reheat food evenly until the core reaches 75 deg C. Do not reheat using hot water, a bain-marie or a lamp. High-risk food (raw and cooked meat, fish, poultry, cooked gravies) must not be cooled and reheated a second time. To cool cooked food for the fridge, bring it from 60 to 21 deg C within 2 hours, and then to 5 deg C within a further 4 hours.
actions: Cool food quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate with date and time.
Check the core temperature with a probe thermometer when reheating.
Do not reheat the same gravy or meat a second time.
caution: Do not serve leftovers to guests if you cannot be sure of how long they were kept.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.4.5, 2.6.1 to 2.6.3
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: I carry packed lunches for guests on a trek. How do I keep food safe?
answer: Part V says hot high-risk food should reach the consumer within 2 hours of preparation, or be kept at 65 deg C if the journey is longer. Chilled food must stay at 5 deg C or below, and frozen food at minus 18 deg C or below. Use clean covered containers, and never use containers that carried garbage, coal or chemicals.
actions: Pack hot food in insulated containers and serve within 2 hours.
Carry cold food in a cool box with ice packs.
Use only food-grade containers kept for food.
caution: In hot weather, avoid taking easily spoiled food (cooked meat, creamy sweets) on long walks.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.9.1 to 2.9.10
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: A guest says they are allergic to nuts. What must I do in my kitchen?
answer: Part V says to know which ingredients have allergens (for example nuts, milk, cereal grains), keep them apart, and stop them getting into other food. Where you cannot be sure of preventing cross-contact, you must inform the guest. For food served for immediate eating, the Labelling rules also expect basic information at the point of sale, including allergen details.
actions: Ask every guest about allergies before you cook.
Use clean separate utensils and boards for allergen-free dishes.
Tell the guest honestly if you cannot guarantee nut-free food.
caution: A serious allergic reaction is an emergency. Call 112 or the local ambulance.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.4.3 and 2.2.9; Labelling and Display Regulations reg 8.4 (prepared food for immediate consumption)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Guests ask for Jain, pure vegetarian or halal food. How should I manage this?
answer: FSSAI Part V requires veg and non-veg food to be stored separately and separate boards to be used. Use the same care for other diet needs: separate pots, spoons and boards. Do not call food Jain, halal or pure veg unless it truly is. I did not find a FSSAI rule on Jain or halal claims, so ask guests what matters to them.
actions: Ask guests in advance what they eat and avoid.
Keep separate utensils, boards and storage for veg and non-veg.
Be honest if you cannot fully meet a diet need.
caution: Halal and Jain claims on packaged food may need other approvals. Check before you print them on labels.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 2.2.5 (segregation of vegetarian and non-vegetarian), 2.3.4 (boards); no FSSAI text on Jain/halal claims found
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Do I have to put the green or brown veg/non-veg mark on my packed products?
answer: Yes for packaged food. Vegetarian food shows a green filled circle inside a green-outlined square. Non-vegetarian food shows a brown filled triangle inside a brown-outlined square. FSSAI says the declaration cannot be exempted, and even packs under 100 sq cm must carry it. It must be on the front of the pack near the product name.
actions: Choose the correct symbol for each product.
Print it on the front of the pack near the name.
caution: Honey is not counted as non-vegetarian in the definition. Ask your office about unusual products.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 5.4; FSSAI FAQ 2023 FAQ 9 and 11
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Which allergens must I write on the label of my snacks and sweets?
answer: Packaged foods must declare these: cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, milk, eggs, fish, peanuts and tree nuts, soybeans, and sulphite (10 mg/kg or more). Use a 'Contains ...' statement. Wording such as 'may contain traces of' is allowed in FSSAI examples. Raw farm products such as peanuts, pulses, rice, fruit, vegetables and spices in unprocessed form are exempted.
actions: List every allergen ingredient in your recipe.
Print a 'Contains ...' line near the ingredients.
caution: If you use a shared pot or board for nuts and other snacks, add the 'may contain' note.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 5.14 (allergen list); FSSAI FAQ 2023 FAQ 5, 23, 29
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What must be written on the label of my homemade pickle, jam or masala packs?
answer: The Labelling Regulations list: name of food, ingredients, nutrition information, veg/non-veg symbol, food additives, maker's name and address, FSSAI logo and licence number, net quantity and price, batch number and date marking. Text must be in English or Hindi (Devanagari). Other languages may be added if they do not contradict English or Hindi. Packs under 100 sq cm are exempt from some items (ingredients, nutrition, lot number, additives and licence number) but not the veg/non-veg mark.
actions: Prepare a label with all required items, check it with your Food Safety Officer.
Print the FSSAI logo and your number in a colour that stands out from the background.
caution: This is a summary. Get the label checked by the office before large printing.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 4.5, 5 and 8.1; FSSAI FAQ 2023 FAQ 2
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I use our local name or dialect for the product on the label?
answer: Yes, you can add another language. The rule says the required details must be in English or Hindi in Devanagari script, and other languages are allowed if they do not contradict the English or Hindi text. Names must not be false or misleading.
actions: Print the required details in English or Hindi first.
Add the local name beside it if you wish.
caution: A local name that suggests a different product or place could be treated as misleading. Ask your office.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 4.5 (English or Hindi in Devanagari; other languages allowed) and 4.3
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I write 'natural', 'pure', 'handmade' or 'traditional recipe' on my pack?
answer: Descriptions must not be false, misleading or deceptive. Claims are also controlled under the separate FSSAI Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018. I did not find a rule on words like 'handmade'. Only write what you can prove, and keep a note of how the product is made.
actions: Write only claims that are true for every batch.
Ask your Food Safety Officer before using words like natural, pure or preservative-free.
caution: False claims can lead to penalties. Do not copy claims from big brands.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 4.3; Advertising and Claims Regulations 2018 referenced in reg 5.1 (not read)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How do I decide the 'best before' date for my pickle or jam?
answer: Best before means the period during which the food stays fully marketable and keeps its qualities, though quality may have fallen after. The law needs date marking on the pack. I could not find an official method for small makers to set shelf life. A safe approach is to test your product in a lab and note storage conditions, and ask your Food Safety Officer.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer how to set shelf life for your product.
Keep your sample batches and test reports.
Write the batch number and date on every pack.
caution: Do not guess shelf life or copy another brand's. Spoiled packed food can harm people.
evidence: Labelling and Display Regulations 2020 reg 2(c) (best before definition) and reg 5.10 (date marking); no method for setting shelf life found
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Are there special FSSAI rules for honey, pickles and spices that we sell?
answer: Many foods have FSSAI product standards. I could not read the standards for honey, pickles or spices this session, so I cannot tell you the limits. The general rules (registration or licence, hygiene, label with FSSAI number, veg symbol) apply. Honey is mentioned in the Labelling Regulations only as not being treated as non-vegetarian.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer for the standard for each product you sell.
Test your product in an FSSAI-recognised lab before selling widely.
caution: Do not mix other sweeteners or colours into honey or spices. That would be adulteration.
evidence: Labelling regs definition 2(o) mention honey; product standards not read this session
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I sell packed local snacks or pickles to guests at my homestay?
answer: Selling food is a food business, so you need the right FSSAI registration or licence. Packaged items need a proper label with the FSSAI number. If you buy from local producers, check that they have an FSSAI number on the pack.
actions: Check your FSSAI category covers sale of packed items.
Buy only from producers who show an FSSAI number.
Keep products in a clean, dry place away from sun.
caution: Selling unlabelled home-made jars to tourists could cause problems if a guest falls ill.
evidence: FSS Act s.3(1)(n) and s.31; Labelling Regulations reg 5.7 (FSSAI logo and licence number)
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I say my vegetables or products are organic?
answer: Organic food must be certified under NPOP or PGS-India, and certified organic food carries the Jaivik Bharat logo and the FSSAI logo and licence number. The FSSAI FAQ says organic food sold directly to the final consumer by the small original producer or a producer organisation is exempt from certification. A single-ingredient product from PGS-India may be labelled 'PGS-Organic'. A multi-ingredient product needs at least 95 per cent certified ingredients for 'Certified Organic'.
actions: Contact your state organic certification office or PGS-India regional council to see how to get certified.
Do not use the word organic on packs or menus until you have certification or a confirmed exemption.
caution: The direct-sale exemption wording is from an undated FSSAI FAQ. An older 2019 relief for small sellers ended on 1 April 2020. Verify the current rule before you rely on it.
evidence: Jaivik Bharat FAQ (FSSAI): NPOP/PGS-India prerequisite; direct-sale exemption; PGS-Organic; 95 per cent rule; Jaivik Bharat logo
verify_with: State organic certification cell / PGS-India regional council; FSSAI helpline

question_en: What is FoSTaC? Do I or my cook need Food Safety Supervisor training?
answer: FoSTaC is FSSAI's Food Safety Training and Certification programme. FSSAI's FoSTaC site says licensed food businesses must have at least one trained and certified Food Safety Supervisor for every 25 food handlers in each premises. Whether a registered small kitchen must have a certified supervisor was not clear in the pages I read.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer if you need a certified supervisor.
Enrol yourself or your head cook on the FoSTaC portal for the right course.
Contact fostac@fssai.gov.in for queries.
caution: Course fees and duration were not shown on the pages I read, so no cost is given. Be careful of private agents who charge unusual amounts.
evidence: FoSTaC portal text: one trained Food Safety Supervisor per 25 food handlers per premises; FSSAI email fostac@fssai.gov.in
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What is the FSSAI Hygiene Rating and can a small village eatery get it?
answer: The Hygiene Rating Scheme gives a 1 to 5 smiley rating to food service places (hotels, restaurants, dhabas, bakeries, meat and sweet shops) based on a third-party audit. You first need an FSSAI registration or licence, follow Schedule 4, and have a FoSTaC-trained Food Safety Supervisor. The rating is valid for two years. Ratings of 3 to 5 are displayed; below 3 you can apply again after 3 months. Audit cost was not stated.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer whether your outlet is eligible.
Get your licence, hygiene, and supervisor training in place first.
caution: Audit fees are paid to approved audit agencies; check the cost with them before you apply.
evidence: FSSAI Hygiene Rating Guidance Document: eligibility, pre-conditions, rating bands, 2-year validity, display
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What is Eat Right India and is there anything useful for villages and tourism?
answer: Eat Right India is FSSAI's national food-safety movement. Its menu lists many initiatives: Street Food Hub, Fruits and Vegetables Market, Station, Place of Worship, Campus, School, Hygiene Rating, Jaivik Bharat, Save Food Share Food, Repurpose Used Cooking Oil, FoSTaC training and a Millets theme. A 2022 FSSAI article says the Clean Street Food Hub targets vendor clusters with training and third-party audits. I did not find a special scheme for tourist or heritage food hubs.
actions: Ask your Food Safety Officer if a Clean Street Food Hub or Hygiene Rating is available near you.
Ask for the state's Eat Right India nodal officer.
caution: Rules and eligibility differ by scheme. Check the Eat Right India website before you plan.
evidence: Eat Right India navigation menu (S45) and FSSAI CEO article June 2022 (S46); no tourism-specific scheme found
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: We want to promote our millet snacks. Does FSSAI support millets or local food fairs?
answer: A 2022 FSSAI article says Eat Right Melas (75 events in India) promote safe, healthy, sustainable diets and highlight millets and local seasonal produce, and that FSSAI encourages whole grains including indigenous grains. The Eat Right India site also has a Millets 2023 section. Millet snacks that you pack and sell still need registration, hygiene and a proper label.
actions: Ask the state food safety office about any Eat Right Mela near you.
Get registration and labels ready before you sell millet snacks.
caution: This is about FSSAI schemes only. Other government schemes for millets are not covered here.
evidence: FSSAI CEO article June 2022 (Eat Right Mela 75 events, millets); Eat Right India menu 'Millets 2023'
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: What should I do with used cooking oil from my kitchen?
answer: Eat Right India has an initiative called Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO), where used oil is collected and turned into biodiesel or soap. I could not read the oil-quality limits or collection rules this session. Do not pour used oil down the drain or reuse oil that is dark or smells bad.
actions: Store used oil in a closed container.
Ask the food safety office whether a RUCO collection agency works in your area.
caution: I could not confirm the official limit for how long oil can be reused. Ask your Food Safety Officer.
evidence: FSSAI CEO article June 2022 (RUCO for biodiesel/soap); Eat Right menu lists RUCO; limits not read
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Guests are vomiting after a meal at my place. What should I do first?
answer: Stop serving the suspect food now. Help sick guests: give them clean water or ORS (oral rehydration solution), keep them comfortable, and get a doctor for anyone who is very sick, a child, elderly or pregnant, or has blood in stool, high fever or cannot keep fluids down. For severe cases call 112 (all-India emergency number, which covers health) or your state ambulance number.
actions: Stop serving the suspect food and set it aside covered; do not throw it away yet.
Call a doctor or 112 for severe cases.
Write down who ate what and when, and the names of people who fell ill.
caution: This is first-aid guidance, not medical advice. Do not give medicine without a doctor's advice.
evidence: 112 India ERSS page (police, fire, health); first-aid steps are general practice
verify_with: Local doctor / District health office; 112 for emergencies

question_en: After guests fell ill, who do I have to tell and should I keep samples?
answer: I could not find an FSSAI page that tells hosts exactly whom to report to after a food-poisoning event. A sensible approach: tell the local health authority or doctor, and your District Food Safety Officer, and cooperate with them. Keep a covered sample of the suspect food, the menu, ingredient purchase receipts and your cleaning records. The Food Safety Officer can take samples under the Act.
actions: Call your District Food Safety Officer and tell them honestly what happened.
Keep the food sample, bills, and staff health records ready.
Give guests your contact and follow up on their recovery.
caution: Do not clean away evidence before the officer sees it, but do not serve the suspect food.
evidence: FSS Act s.38 (FSO may take samples); no FSSAI incident-reporting text found; practice-based
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / District health office / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: How do I talk to guests when they fall ill after eating at my place?
answer: Be calm, kind and honest. Say you are sorry that they are unwell, help them get care first, and do not blame them. Do not hide the facts. Share what you are doing (stopping the food, informing the office). Keep a written record of what you said and did.
actions: Help the guest see a doctor first.
Tell the guest what you are doing to find the cause.
Write a short incident note with date, time, menu and people affected.
caution: Avoid promising money or taking blame in a way that has legal effect without advice. Ask a local lawyer or your insurer if there is a dispute.
evidence: General hospitality practice; guests' right to test under FSS Act s.40
verify_with: Insurer / local lawyer / District Food Safety Officer

question_en: Can I serve wine, beer or local liquor to my guests?
answer: Alcohol is not covered by an FSSAI registration. Liquor sale and service need a licence under your state's excise law. For example, the Delhi Excise Department lists many licence types under the Delhi Excise Act, 2009; other states have their own Acts and rules. Do not serve or sell alcohol to guests without the right state licence.
actions: Ask your District Excise Office whether any licence is possible for your homestay.
Do not sell or serve liquor until you have the licence in writing.
caution: Rules differ by state, and penalties can be serious. Ask the excise office before you plan any alcohol service.
evidence: Delhi Excise Department page (state Act and licence classes) as an example; FSS Act s.3 lists alcoholic drink within 'food' but licensing is under state excise law (general principle)
verify_with: District Excise Office of your state

question_en: In my cooking class guests chop and cook. How do I keep this safe and hygienic?
answer: Give a short hygiene briefing at the start: wash hands with soap, tie hair, remove rings, cover cuts, and no one with stomach illness should join. Keep guest tasks to low-risk jobs where possible and watch raw meat handling. Part V rules on handwashing, boards, temperatures and allergens apply to your kitchen. Ask about allergies before the class.
actions: Provide a handwashing station and show guests how to use it.
Give each guest a clean apron and board.
Ask about allergies and illness before the class begins.
caution: Keep hot stoves and sharp knives safe for guests, especially children.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V personal hygiene, allergen control, boards and temperatures; briefing structure is general practice
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Should I have insurance in case a guest gets ill or hurt in my kitchen or cooking class?
answer: Insurance is not an FSSAI requirement that I could verify. Many hosts consider public liability insurance for guest injury and illness claims. Ask an insurance company or agent what cover fits a homestay or an activity that serves food, and what the policy excludes.
actions: Ask two insurers what cover they offer for homestays serving food.
Read the exclusions and keep your licence and records in order, as insurers may ask for them.
caution: I did not verify any scheme, premium or product. Ask a licensed insurer.
evidence: General practice; no official source on insurance read
verify_with: Licensed insurance company or agent

question_en: Can I serve wild mushrooms or foraged greens that we collect from the forest to guests?
answer: Wrongly identified mushrooms and plants can cause serious poisoning. I did not find an FSSAI rule on foraged foods this session. Do not serve wild mushrooms or unknown plants to paying guests unless an expert from your community has identified them and you are sure. Forest collection may also need permission from the Forest Department or the community.
actions: Serve only foods your family has always eaten safely and can identify without doubt.
Ask the Forest Department and your community whether collection is allowed.
caution: If a guest becomes ill after eating wild food, get urgent medical help and keep a sample.
evidence: No official source read for foraged foods; FSS Act s.26 duty of FBO not to sell unsafe food; general safety practice
verify_with: Forest Department; local agriculture or health office

question_en: I serve vegetables from my own field. How do I make sure there is no pesticide risk?
answer: I could not verify FSSAI limits for pesticide residue this session. A safe practice: follow the label waiting period between spraying and harvest, keep spray records, store chemicals away from food, and wash vegetables well in clean water before cooking. Ask your agriculture department or Krishi Vigyan Kendra about safe use.
actions: Keep a spray diary with dates, chemicals and harvest dates.
Wash vegetables in clean, safe water before use.
Ask your Krishi Vigyan Kendra about safe pesticide use.
caution: Do not wash or mix pesticide tools in the kitchen or in the water source used for drinking.
evidence: General practice; Part V water and storage rules for ingredients; no pesticide limits read
verify_with: Krishi Vigyan Kendra / State agriculture department

question_en: What drinking water should I give guests? Can I serve tap, well or filtered water?
answer: Give only water you know is safe. FSSAI says water for drinking, cooking and ice should meet the BIS IS 10500 drinking-water standard. Test your source (see the water testing row). Boil, filter or treat water if the test shows any problem. If you buy bottled water, buy a sealed pack that shows the FSSAI logo and number, and check the date.
actions: Test your water source at least twice a year.
Keep drinking water in clean covered containers.
Offer sealed packaged water if you are unsure.
caution: A filter alone may not remove all germs or chemicals. Ask the lab what is in your water.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V 1.4.1 (IS 10500); Labelling regs (FSSAI logo and licence number on pack); I could not read packaged drinking water rules
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: Can I serve fresh milk from our own cow or buffalo to guests?
answer: Milk is a high-risk food. FSSAI keeps full hygiene and testing rules for dairy even in the 2026 reform. I did not read milk-specific rules this session, so I cannot give a legal answer on raw milk. A safe practice is to boil milk well before serving it. Ask your Food Safety Officer if you sell or supply milk regularly, as milk sellers need registration or licence.
actions: Boil milk fully before serving it to guests.
Keep milking and storage containers clean and covered.
Ask the Food Safety Officer if you sell milk.
caution: FSSAI FAQ says milk sellers need registration; a vendor who supplies his whole milk to a registered cooperative society is exempt. Check which case applies to you.
evidence: FSSAI FAQs 27 Mar 2026 Q15 (dairy keeps full hygiene rules); FAQ 2022 Q87, Q89; boil-milk advice is general practice
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

topic: What to do first on food safety
question_en: I am new to this. What are the five most important food safety things I should do first?
answer: Start with these: (1) clean safe water, (2) handwashing with soap for everyone who cooks, (3) keep raw and cooked food apart and covered, (4) cook food hot enough and keep it hot or cold (hot at 65 deg C or above, cold at 5 deg C or below), (5) keep sick people out of the kitchen. Then check what FSSAI registration you need.
actions: Fix water and handwashing today.
Buy a probe thermometer and use it for meat and reheated food.
Call your Food Safety Officer to confirm your registration.
caution: Hygiene rules apply whether or not you are already registered.
evidence: FSSAI 2018 notice Part V and Part I basics
verify_with: District Food Safety Officer / FSSAI helpline 1800112100

question_en: For food questions, which office or number do I use for licence, water, alcohol, organic and medical help?
answer: Licence, hygiene and inspection: your District Food Safety Officer, or the FSSAI helpline 1800112100. Water testing: your Gram Panchayat or the water supply office (Jal Jeevan Mission system). Alcohol: your state excise office. Organic: your state organic certification cell or PGS-India council. Emergencies: 112.
actions: Save 1800112100 and 112 in your phone.
Write the names and numbers of your local offices in a small notebook.
caution: Office names differ by state. Check yours.
evidence: FSSAI helpdesk; JJM WQMIS; state excise page; Jaivik Bharat FAQ; 112 India page
verify_with: Your district administration
